articles.title: Martlet Kitchen at Rochdale Town Hall Wins Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Award 2026
articles.excerpt: The Martlet Kitchen, located in Rochdale Town Hall, has received the Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Award for 2026, recognising its commitment to quality and local sourcing.
articles.content_html:
The Martlet Kitchen, situated within Rochdale Town Hall, has been awarded the Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Award for 2026. This accolade places the restaurant among the top 10 percent of listings on the popular travel platform, highlighting its dedication to quality and customer satisfaction.

Chef Darren Parkinson, who has previously worked at renowned establishments such as Shibden Mill Inn and Fleece Inn, leads the kitchen at the Martlet Kitchen. The restaurant is known for its focus on British cuisine, sourcing ingredients from local suppliers to create a menu that is regularly updated. Notable dishes include fish and chips, and the restaurant also features a grill club on Fridays and fine dining on Saturday evenings.

Sarah Crabtree serves as the restaurant manager, overseeing a team that prides itself on delivering excellent service. The Martlet Kitchen also offers private dining options in the Mayor’s reception room, catering to various events and gatherings.

Darren Parkinson aims to achieve further accolades in the future, building on the restaurant's reputation for consistent positive reviews. The Martlet Kitchen's recognition by Tripadvisor underscores its commitment to providing a high-quality dining experience in a Grade I listed building.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Moves Forward with Hopwood Hall Redevelopment After High Court Ruling
articles.excerpt: Following a High Court ruling, Rochdale Council has confirmed plans to redevelop Hopwood Hall, with an emphasis on community use, after ending an exclusivity agreement with Hopwood DePree.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has announced its commitment to the redevelopment of Hopwood Hall following a recent High Court ruling that upheld the council's decision to terminate an exclusivity agreement with American filmmaker Hopwood DePree. The ruling, delivered at Manchester Civil Justice Centre, concluded that the council acted lawfully when it ended the agreement, which had been in place since 2017.

The council leader, Neil Emmott, addressed the future of the historic building during a town hall meeting on October 15, stating that the council is focused on bringing Hopwood Hall back into use for the community. Emmott expressed openness to DePree's involvement, indicating that if he presents a viable plan, the council would consider it. However, he noted that the legal process is not yet concluded, as DePree has the option to appeal the decision by November 18, 2026, with a potential extension to November 28, 2026.

The High Court's decision came after DePree claimed he had a legally binding agreement to purchase the hall for £1, based on a planning approval granted in 2022. However, the court found that this approval did not trigger the option to purchase. The council has already invested over £1.6 million in repairs to the hall, and Emmott assured that any costs awarded to the council, amounting to £114,000, would be reinvested into the project.

As the situation develops, the council remains committed to the restoration and preservation of Hopwood Hall, which is seen as a valuable asset for the local community. Emmott reiterated that the council's focus is on securing the hall's long-term future, and the outcome of any potential appeal will be crucial in determining the next steps.

The two day trial in Manchester Civil Justice Centre ruled that the council was not acting unlawfully when it ended an exclusivity agreement with the American filmmaker. ‌ Mr DePree entered an option agreement with the council to restore the hall back in 2017, until that agreement was ended in October 2024. Since then, Mr DePree, who claims ancestral connections with the 1400s stately home, has felt he had a legally binding agreement to purchase Hopwood Hall for £1. ‌ Click here for the latest on Greater Manchester's politics in our newsletter The High Court found that the ‘change of use’ planning approval was granted in 2022 wasn’t enough to trigger the option to purchase the hall for a ‘peppercorn fee’ – £1. In response to Coun Steve Potter’s question about the next steps for Hopwood Hall, Coun Emmott said: “The High Court’s judgment in relation to Hopwood Hall does not necessarily mark the end of the legal process. ‌ “Mr DePree has the right to seek permission to appeal the decision. The court has directed that any application for permission to appeal must be lodged by November 18, 2026, although there is scope for this deadline to be extended to November 28, 2026. “The council was awarded total costs of £114,000. I can confirm these monies will be reinvested into the project. As part of any appeal process, Mr DePree would be required to make a payment into court of approximately £80,000 towards Rochdale council ’s legal costs. This would require him to demonstrate that the proposed appeal has a real prospect of success or that there is another compelling reason for it to be heard. “Only Mr DePree and his legal advisers can determine whether an appeal is pursued. It is understandable that emotions remain strong within the local community, particularly among those volunteers who have dedicated considerable time and effort to the Hopwood Hall project. However, the council cannot move forward until the matter of the appeal is settled. We will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. “Whatever the future holds for Hopwood Hall, this building, once restored and refurbished, will be used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton’s rich and varied heritage.” Mr DePree has not mentioned whether his team will appeal the decision or not. articles.title: Court Rules on Ownership Dispute Over Hopwood Hall
articles.excerpt: A High Court ruling has denied Hopwood DePree's claim to ownership of Hopwood Hall, concluding that Rochdale Council acted fairly in its decision to end the exclusivity agreement.
articles.content_html:
A High Court in Manchester has ruled against Hopwood DePree in his bid to gain ownership of Hopwood Hall, a historic manor house in Rochdale. The ruling concluded that Rochdale Council acted fairly when it ended an exclusivity agreement with DePree, who is a descendant of the family that originally built the hall in the 1420s.

The two-day trial, which concluded on 20 October 2026, centred on DePree's claim that the council had reneged on an agreement allowing him to purchase the Grade II-listed property. The council had previously worked with DePree for seven years to facilitate repairs on the dilapidated site, which is now part of Hopwood Hall College. However, in November 2024, the council stated it would explore other options, citing a lack of a commercially viable business model from DePree.

Following the court's decision, DePree expressed disappointment, stating that the ruling was a significant setback for both his family and the community. He indicated that he and his legal team are considering their options moving forward, while also pledging to monitor the council's efforts to restore the hall for public benefit.

Hopwood Hall has a rich history, having been owned by the Hopwood family until 1922, after which it changed hands several times and fell into disrepair. The council acquired the property in the 1980s and has since been responsible for its maintenance.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Court rules in ownership row over Hopwood Hall - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Court rules in ownership row over Hopwood Hall A court has ruled that Rochdale Council did not act unfairly in its decision not to pass ownership of Hopwood Hall to one of its descendants. Today marked the end of a two-day trial in the High Court in Manchester after Hopwood DePree took legal action against the council which ended an exclusivity agreement to sell the historic Grade II-listed hall to him. Following the decision, Mr DePree said: “This is of course incredibly disappointing and a huge blow to our community, our supporters around the world, as well as the UK’s charitable heritage rescue groups in general. “However, please know that my team and I are already determining our legal options and next steps. “We will be watching closely to keep an eye on Rochdale Borough Council’s efforts to save Hopwood Hall for the community, and restore it to its former glory.” Mr DePree is a descendant of the Hopwood family which build the manor house in the 1420s. The family owned the hall and surrounding land — which is now Hopwood Hall College — until 1922. The house was sold 20 years later. It was occupied by a variety of temporary residents, including the de la Salle Brothers, who ran it as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s. It had fallen into disrepair and was bought by Rochdale Council, which still owns the Grade II-listed property. READ MORE:Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026 Finalists Announced Mr DePree launched legal action after he spent seven years working with the council to carry out vital repairs on the dilapidated site with a view to purchasing it. In November, 2024, the council ended its exclusivity agreement with Mr DePree, and said it would explore other options because no “commercially viable” business model had been presented. Mr DePree and volunteers who worked on the hall have been barred from returning to the site since then. In the meantime, the council has spent £640,000 making the roof watertight. A council spokesperson said: “We are pleased with today’s judgement. It’s a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested into this process could have been better spent on the hall itself. “We’re now focussed on moving forward. More than £1.6 million has been spent on the hall by ourselves and Historic England since 2017 and we will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. “Feasibility studies have already been completed and options for Hopwood Hall’s long-term future will be considered in due course. “Whatever the future holds for Hopwood Hall, this building, once restored and refurbished, will be used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton’s rich and varied heritage.” SUPPORT THE ROCHDALE TIMES: FOLLOW US ON FACEBOOK Got a story?
